'''Ana R. Guadalupe Quiñones''' (born 1956) is a Puerto Rican chemist and academic administrator who served as the chancellor of the [[University of Puerto Rico, Río Piedras Campus]] from 2009 to 2013. She researches [[electrochemistry]], specifically in the development of electrochemical sensors, [[biosensor]]s, and [[electrocatalyst]]s for applications in [[bioelectrochemistry]] and [[environmental monitoring]].

== Early life and education ==
Guadalupe was born in 1956.<ref name=":2" /> She attended the [[University of Puerto Rico, Río Piedras Campus]] (UPR-RP).<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Guadalupe Quiñones |first=Ana R. |date=August 17, 2010 |title=CV |url=https://senado.uprrp.edu/comites/Consulta2010/N-ARGuadalupe-Curriculum.pdf |access-date=2024-10-20 |website=University of Puerto Rico, Río Piedras Campus}}</ref> She earned a B.Sc. in chemistry in 1979 and a M.Sc. in [[analytical chemistry]] in 1984.<ref name=":0" /> Her master's thesis was titled, ''Polymer-Modified Electrodes: Electrochemical Characterization and Analytical Applications for the Extraction of Metal Species in Aqueous Solutions''.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Guadalupe Quiñones |first=Ana R. |title=Polymer-Modified Electrodes: Electrochemical Characterization and Analytical Applications for the Extraction of Metal Species in Aqueous Solutions |date=1984 |degree=M.Sc. |publisher=University of Puerto Rico |oclc=24923384}}</ref> Between 1979 and 1981, Guadalupe worked as a laboratory instructor at the [[Universidad del Sagrado Corazón]].<ref name=":0" /> She was a teaching assistant at UPR-RP, from 1981 to 1984.<ref name=":0" />

In 1987, Guadalupe completed a Ph.D. in analytical chemistry, specializing in electrochemistry, at [[Cornell University]].<ref name=":0" /> Her doctoral research focused on the [[electrochemical]] properties of [[chemically modified electrode]]s.<ref name=":0" /> Her dissertation was titled, ''Polymer Modified Electrodes: Electrochemical Characterization and Applications''.<ref name=":2">{{Cite thesis |last=Guadalupe |first=Ana R. |title=Polymer Modified Electrodes: Electrochemical Characterization and Applications |date=1987 |degree=Ph.D. |publisher=Cornell University |oclc=881013391}}</ref> [[Héctor D. Abruña]] was her doctoral advisor.<ref name=":2" /> She completed a postdoctoral fellowship in [[bioelectrochemistry]] at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] from 1987 to 1988.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==

In 1988, Guadalupe became an assistant professor of chemistry at UPR-RP.<ref name=":0" /> Her research during this period focused on electrochemical processes, specifically the study of redox reactions and the development of electrochemical sensors.<ref name=":0" /> In 1989, she joined a collaborative project on the use of polymer-modified electrodes in bioelectrochemical applications, which laid the groundwork for her later research on biosensors.<ref name=":0" /> From 1988 to 1992, she was also an instructor at [[Interamerican University of Puerto Rico]].<ref name=":0" /> She investigated sensor technology, working on the [[Electrocatalyst|electrocatalytic]] oxidation of [[Malic acid|malate]] and [[Lactic acid|lactate]] using [[Ruthenium compounds|ruthenium complexes]], and the development of biosensors for the detection of compounds like [[nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide]] (NADH).<ref name=":0" />

Guadalupe was promoted to associate professor in 1992 at UPR-RP, where she continued her work on electrochemical sensors and biosensors.<ref name=":0" /> Her research during this time included projects on [[polymer]]-supported electrodes, the controlled release of insulin, and the use of ruthenium complexes as molecular probes for enzyme-coupled reactions.<ref name=":0" /> By the mid-1990s, she was recognized for her expertise in bioelectrochemistry and had secured grants from the [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) and the [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF).<ref name=":0" /> In 1994, Guadalupe was appointed coordinator of the UPR-RP chemistry graduate program, a position she held until 1998.<ref name=":0" /> During this period, she supervised a number of graduate theses and expanded her research into areas such as the electrochemical production of [[nanoparticle]]s and their application in catalysis.<ref name=":0" />

In 1998, Guadalupe was promoted to professor of chemistry.<ref name=":0" /> Her work on electrochemical materials and [[nanostructure]]d polymers garnered further recognition, and she began collaborating on interdisciplinary projects involving [[materials science]] and sensor technology.<ref name=":0" /> She also served as president of the Puerto Rico Science Teachers Association from 1991 to 1993 and was a member of the [[American Chemical Society]], where she held various leadership roles, including president of the Puerto Rico chapter in 1998.<ref name=":0" /> From 2001 to 2009, she served as dean of graduate studies and research at UPR-RP, where she was responsible for overseeing the university's research initiatives and securing funding for projects in science and technology.<ref name=":0" /> During this time, she continued her research on electrochemical sensors and biosensors, contributing to advances in detecting environmental pollutants and pathogens like ''[[Salmonella]]''.<ref name=":0" />

In October 2009, Guadalupe was appointed acting chancellor of the UPR-RP.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2021-07-18 |title=Ana Guadalupe, exrectora del Recinto de Río Piedras, entre los candidatos para presidir la UPR |url=https://www.metro.pr/pr/noticias/2021/07/18/ana-guadalupe-exrectora-del-recinto-rio-piedras-los-candidatos-presidir-la-upr.html |access-date=2024-10-20 |website=Metro Puerto Rico |language=es}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2011 |title=Biography |url=https://camarapr.org/SummitE3/BiosE3/Bios-E3-Ana-Guadalupe.pdf |access-date=2024-10-20 |website=Puerto Rico Chamber of Commerce |archive-date=2025-02-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250223061807/https://camarapr.org/SummitE3/BiosE3/Bios-E3-Ana-Guadalupe.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> In this role, she provided leadership during a transitional period for the university, focusing on strengthening research and academic programs.<ref name=":0" /> Her tenure coincided with student protests from 2010 to 2011, sparked by an {{USD|800|2010}} annual fee imposed by the [[University of Puerto Rico]] (UPR) board of trustees.<ref name=":1" /> Guadalupe called for [[Puerto Rico Police|police intervention]] during these protests, leading to violent confrontations and arrests, which drew widespread criticism from the student body.<ref name=":1" /> In March 2011, she was physically and verbally attacked by students, further intensifying the tensions.<ref name=":1" /> She resigned in May 2013 following a reconfiguration of the university's board of trustees.<ref name=":1" /> Her research in the period included the development of electrochemical materials and biosensors for [[environmental monitoring]] and [[public health]] applications.<ref name=":0" /> She also worked on projects involving the electrochemical characterization of [[porous silicon]] and the design of sensors for detecting [[waterborne disease]]s.<ref name=":0" />

In 2021, Guadalupe was considered for the interim presidency of UPR, but her candidacy was met with opposition from students due to her controversial role during the protests.<ref name=":1" /> She was ultimately not selected as a finalist.<ref name=":1" />
